So today, I want to talk about William Grant Still, an American composer sometimes called the Dean of African American Composers. Still grew up in Little Rock, Arkansas. His father, who was a local bandmaster, passed away when Still was just an infant. But his stepfather really nurtured his love of music. He bought recordings of classical operas for the boy and took him to live performances regularly. That early exposure made a huge impression. Still eventually studied at the Oberlin Conservatory of Music, where he learned composition and theory rooted in the European classical tradition. He also studied privately with the avant-garde French composer, Edgard Vérez. So he had this really interesting blend of influences, traditional European form on one hand, and experimental modern techniques on the other. Now, his most celebrated work is the Afro-American Symphony, completed in 1931. This piece is warm and lyrical. It draws heavily on blues melodies and spirituals, and there's a beautiful balance between those folk elements and the formal structure of a classical symphony. It really captures the emotional landscape of everyday African-American life, but still also explored more dramatic territory. His ballet, Sargi, set in Africa, was composed after extensive study of African musical traditions. It uses layered percussion and choral singing to depict a ceremonial scene. Critics regarded it as a powerful expression of cultural heritage and identity.

All right, let's talk about something fascinating. How very young children understand numbers. This is a topic that has kept researchers busy for decades because it tells us so much about how the human mind develops. So one classic experiment is the dot comparison task. Researchers showed toddlers, around three years old, two cards. One card had, say, five dots, and the other had 15. And what they found was that even before these children could count reliably, they could point to the card with more dots. In other words, they had an intuitive sense of quantity, a basic number sense, without any formal instruction. OK, so a second experiment took a different approach. This one used what we call the violation of expectation method, with even younger babies, around five months old. Here's how it worked. Babies watched as one toy was placed on a small stage, then a screen went up, and a second toy was added behind it. When the screen dropped, sometimes it revealed two toys, which is correct, and sometimes it showed just one. The babies stared significantly longer at the unexpected result, the single toy, which suggests they expected 1 plus 1 to equal 2. So basically babies are intuitive mathematicians. They seem to grasp basic quantities from very early on. Now the question is, does this early number sense connect to other kinds of abstract reasoning? Let's look at some research exploring that connection.

So when people hear the words public transit, they often think about crowded buses, delays, noise, basically all the negative stuff. And sure, poorly managed systems can contribute to pollution and congestion. However, when cities invest wisely in their transit networks, the results can actually be surprisingly positive for the environment. Take Bogota, Columbia, for example. In the early 2000s, the city built a bus rapid transit system with dedicated lanes and efficient stations. The result? Many residents who previously drove chose to ride the bus instead. This cut down on traffic congestion and noticeably improved air quality in the city center. Now contrast that with car-dependent suburban areas. When neighborhoods are spread out, everyone needs a private vehicle. That means more fuel consumption, more roads to build and maintain, and infrastructure costs stretched across a huge area. So paradoxically, those quiet suburban neighborhoods can actually have a larger environmental footprint per person than a dense city with well-designed transit. And here's another interesting case. Seoul has been converting elevated highways into green parks in pedestrian zones. On this freed up space for community gardens where residents grow food locally. As a result, these neighborhoods have reduced their dependence on produce shipped in from distant farms. So the takeaway is this. Thoughtful investment in public transit and urban redesign can make dense cities significantly greener than low density suburbs.

Okay, so today I want to talk about something pretty remarkable. How ancient Polynesian sailors navigated thousands of miles across the open Pacific Ocean without any of the instruments we think of as essential for sea travel. No compasses, no maps, no written charts. And yet, they managed to settle islands scattered across an enormous stretch of ocean. So how did they do it? Well, Polynesian navigators relied on what we call wayfinding. Basically, they read natural signs. They memorized the positions of hundreds of stars at different times of year and used them as a kind of celestial guide. But it wasn't just stars. They also paid close attention to ocean swell patterns, the way waves reflected off distant islands could signal that land was nearby, even before they could actually see it. And they watched the flight paths of certain seabirds, since some species fly out to sea during the day, but always return to land at night. Now, the evidence for how widely they traveled is really impressive. Archaeologists have found similar styles of pottery, the same cultivated plants like taro and breadfruit, and closely related languages on islands thousands of miles apart. All of this points to a connected network of voyagers who deliberately explored and colonized new territories. What's really significant here is that this challenges the old assumption that long-distance ocean travel required advanced technology. These navigators achieved extraordinary feats through careful observation and knowledge passed down across generations.
